html:
The map's label, used for 2000 BCE, for the peoples of North America who lived by hunting, fishing and gathering in the long period archaeologists call the Archaic, roughly 8000 to 1000 BCE.

After the Ice Age the mammoths and other big game were gone, and people used a much wider range of food: deer, fish, shellfish, nuts, seeds and roots. They hunted with spears thrown from a spear-thrower, ground seeds and nuts on stones, and many groups moved between camps by season.

In the eastern woodlands some groups began to tend squash, sunflower and other local seed plants, the start of the Eastern Agricultural Complex. Some built earthworks long before farming took hold, among them Poverty Point in Louisiana around 1700 BCE. Later cultures such as the Adena grew out of this world, and many regions kept a foraging life for much longer, as the desert foragers of the west did.
